State-based decoding of hand and finger kinematics using neuronal ensemble and LFP activity in motor cortex
Rebecca J. Flint; Nitish V. Thakor; Nitish V. Aggarwal; Matthew C. Oby; Lee E. Miller
Summary: This paper introduces a **two-stage, state-based decoding framework** in which local field potential (LFP) features from motor cortex first classify behavioral epochs (baseline, reaction, movement, hold), and this LFP-based state decoder then *triggers* a spike-based Kalman filter to continuously decode 3D hand position plus 18 wrist and finger joint angles during reach-to-grasp movements.[1] By optimally combining LFPs for autonomous state switching with spikes for high-fidelity kinematics, the approach significantly improves decoding accuracy over spike-only decoders and provides a more robust, behavior-aware control strategy. For biorobotics, this architecture offers a practical way to achieve **stable, multi-DOF neuroprosthetic and robotic hand control**, minimizing unintended movements during posture while enhancing fine finger and grasp kinematics during active movement.[1]

**Hendrik M. Out; Nico Vos; Laura Nishimura; Fabian J.F. van der Helm; Eftychios A. Psomopoulos; Reza Sharif Razavian; Vivian K. Mushahwar; Sander M. Neggers; Mischa W. P. Hendriks**[2]
Summary: The paper systematically characterizes how **surface EMG (sEMG) signal properties change after traumatic spinal cord injury**, showing consistent alterations in amplitude, timing, spectral content, and motor unit behavior that reflect residual but re-organized spinal motor commands.[5] Its key innovation is to reinterpret these altered sEMG features as **informative biomarkers of residual motor command and neuromuscular integrity**, providing a structured framework for decoding motor intent in “clinically complete” SCI where conventional assessments see no function.[5] For biorobotics, this positions multi‑channel and high‑density sEMG as a rich control and feedback modality for neuroprostheses and exoskeletons, enabling more sensitive motor decoding, adaptive controllers, and personalized rehabilitation strategies that exploit subtle residual descending drive rather than relying solely on overt voluntary movement.
